🐛 Describe the bug
Change model size or load weights will cause multiprocessing deadlock. But WHY? Below are one case.
import multiprocessing
import torch 
import torch.nn as nn 
 
# Change the hidden from 128 to 6 will erase the stuck?
strange_hidden = 128

lstm = nn.LSTM(input_size=2, hidden_size=strange_hidden, num_layers=1, batch_first=True)
torch.save(lstm.state_dict(),"./plain.pt") 

def run(inputs): 
    model = nn.LSTM(input_size=2, hidden_size=strange_hidden, num_layers=1, batch_first=True)
    model.load_state_dict(torch.load("./plain.pt")) 
    x=model(inputs) 
    return x 

state=torch.rand(1,1,2) 
print("CHECKPOINT 0 PASS")

# Comment the line below will erase the stuck
lstm.load_state_dict(torch.load("./plain.pt"))
# Comment the line above will erase the stuck
# What is weird, if I change the strange hidden_size from 128 to 6, it would never stuck!


x = lstm(state)
print(x[0].shape)
print("CHECKPOINT 1 PASS")

pool = multiprocessing.Pool(5)
for i in range(5):
    pool.apply_async(func=run,args=(state,))
pool.close()
pool.join()
print("CHECKPOINT 2 PASS")

Strange bug or I made some mistake? I tried on muliple pytorch version, it is still the same. And it is noticed the number 90 is special? Set hidden size below 90 will erase the deadlock.

📚 The doc issue
requesting to add FlopCounterMode documentation
and to include the following notes from these discussion:


https://pytorch.slack.com/archives/C3PDTEV8E/p1712785539175899 (elementwise ops aren't counted - and why)


https://pytorch.slack.com/archives/C3PDTEV8E/p1712798211869749?thread_ts=1712786199.970369&cid=C3PDTEV8E  torch.compile usage: the intended usage is to use it on an uncompiled version of the model first.


the mode counts only matmul, conv, attn - may be a few other high intense blocks, but it doesn't count almost anything else (not sin, mul, any element-wise ops). Perhaps  the best advice to add here would be to use FlopCounterMode(display=True) while debugging since it gives the exact breakdown of which ops it measured - which means everything else is ignored.


document that it will not count custom kernels and how to make it count those (register FLOP formulas for them)


let's perhaps include the very cool integration Lightning folks (Carlos Mocholi et al) did using the meta-model: https://pytorch.slack.com/archives/C3PDTEV8E/p1712788665140289?thread_ts=1712786199.970369&cid=C3PDTEV8E - may be this could be a util provided by pytorch? (edit: when tried this is practice - apparently this meta device solution will often fail if an op isn't implemented on meta.)



mar-2025 update: Additionally the user needs to be aware that running FlopCounterMode incurs a significant overhead in both compute and memory usage - which renders it unusable in many use cases where gpu memory is tight. Compute isn't a problem if the result is cached, but memory usage overhead leads to OOM when FlopCounterMode is run and the memory was close to being full.
tag: @Chillee
cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @kadeng @msaroufim @svekars @sekyondaMeta @AlannaBurke @brycebortree

🐛 Describe the bug
import torch
torch.set_default_device('cuda')

@torch.compile(fullgraph=True)
def f(x):
    x = x.cos().cos()
    print(x)
    return x.cos()

def g(x):
    return f(x)

torch.compiler.disable(g)(torch.randn(5))

This still compiles (and throws the error).
Also, the docstring also claims it can be used as a context manager, but this error is thrown when you try to use it that way.

nodes.bodyText:
📚 The doc issue
A bit of context:
When I tried to port code that has F.interpolate from cpu to mps, I saw this error.
Adaptive pool MPS: input sizes must be divisible by output sizes.

Before finding #96056, I expected this op should behave exactly the same, so I thought it's a bug in PyTorch.
If we can't expect ops behave exactly the same (I don't mean precision-wise), I think we can add more notes about behavior discrepancies to the documentation.
Suggest a potential alternative/fix
I think at least when throwing errors that are specific to devices, PyTorch should point to tracking issues.
cc @kulinseth @albanD @malfet @DenisVieriu97 @jhavukainen

🐛 Describe the bug
I'm trying to change .requires_grad status inside the function that gets compiled, but it doesn't work. Without compiling it works. Here's the code that reproduces the problem:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class SimpleNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, output_size):
        super(SimpleNN, self).__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size)
        self.activation = nn.ReLU()
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, output_size)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.fc1(x)
        x = self.activation(x)
        x = self.fc2(x)
        return x
    

def task(model_1, model_2, input, target_output):
    # Forward pass
    with torch.no_grad():
        intermediate_output = model_1(input)
    intermediate_output.requires_grad_()
    print(intermediate_output.requires_grad) # prints false if doing task = torch.compile(task), true if not
    output = model_2(intermediate_output)
    loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()
    loss = loss_fn(output, target_data)
    return loss


# Subsequent modules test
input_size = 1 # xy location
hidden_size = 32
output_size = 1 # rgb 

model_1 = SimpleNN(input_size, hidden_size, output_size)
model_2 = SimpleNN(input_size, hidden_size, output_size)

# Creating random input and target tensors
torch.manual_seed(42)  # For reproducibility
N = 100  # Batch size
input_data = torch.randn(N, input_size)
target_data = torch.randn(N, output_size)

🐛 Describe the bug
TL;DR: I want to be able to call a function like TensorImpl::may_have_symbolic_sizes_strides() which will never return false if the tensor contains symbolic sizes / strides. Today, we have TensorImpl::has_symbolic_sizes_strides() which doesn't obey this property - in the repro at the bottom of this issue, we have an example of a Nested Tensor with symbolic sizes for which has_symbolic_sizes_strides() returns False. My question - what's the right way to provide this API?
Background: has_symbolic_sizes_strides vs python-implemented sizes:
has_symbolic_sizes_strides is set to true if, during construction of a TensorImpl, symbolic sizes are passed in:

  
    
      pytorch/c10/core/TensorImpl.cpp
    
    
        Lines 852 to 866
      in
      56dd760
    
  
  
    

        
          
           if (int_sizes && int_strides && 
        

        
          
               // NB: storage_offset guaranteed to be positive 
        

        
          
               (!storage_offset.has_value() || !storage_offset->is_heap_allocated()) && 
        

        
          
               !has_symbolic_sizes_strides_) { 
        

        
          
             set_sizes_and_strides(*int_sizes, *int_strides); 
        

        
          
             if (storage_offset.has_value()) 
        

        
          
               set_storage_offset(storage_offset->as_int_unchecked()); 
        

        
          
             return; 
        

        
          
           } 
        

        
          
           TORCH_CHECK( 
        

        
          
               allow_tensor_metadata_change(), 
        

        
          
               "set_sizes_and_strides ", 
        

        
          
               err_msg_tensor_metadata_change_not_allowed); 
        

        
          
            
        

        
          
           has_symbolic_sizes_strides_ = true; 
        
    
  


But in the case of tensor subclasses, we can provide the option to implement sizes/strides in python. Nested Tensor uses this option, in the 2nd input to _make_wrapper_subclass. Additionally, the 11th input is "sizes", which implies something (described below)

  
    
      pytorch/torch/nested/_internal/nested_tensor.py
    
    
        Lines 64 to 74
      in
      56dd760
    
  
  
    

        
          
           r = torch.Tensor._make_wrapper_subclass(  # type: ignore[attr-defined] 
        

        
          
               cls, 
        

        
          
               (0,), 
        

        
          
               (0,), 
        

        
          
               0, 
        

        
          
               torch.contiguous_format, 
        

        
          
               values.dtype, 
        

        
          
               torch.jagged, 
        

        
          
               values.device, 
        

        
          
               False, 
        

        
          
               kwargs.get("requires_grad", False), 
        
    
  


The 11th input of "sizes" is the dispatch_sizes_strides_policy:

  
    
      pytorch/torch/csrc/autograd/python_variable.cpp
    
    
         Line 753
      in
      56dd760
    
  
  
    

        
          
           "c10::string_view? dispatch_sizes_strides_policy=None, bool dispatch_device=False, bool dispatch_layout=False, " 
        
    
  


we use it to set_python_custom_sizes_strides; in this case, "sizes" gets parsed to c10::TensorImpl::SizesStridesPolicy::CustomSizes

  
    
      pytorch/torch/csrc/autograd/python_variable.cpp
    
    
         Line 753
      in
      56dd760
    
  
  
    

        
          
           "c10::string_view? dispatch_sizes_strides_policy=None, bool dispatch_device=False, bool dispatch_layout=False, " 
        
    
  


following this pointer to set_python_custom_sizes_strides:

  
    
      pytorch/c10/core/TensorImpl.h
    
    
        Lines 2779 to 2782
      in
      56dd760
    
  
  
    

        
          
           void set_python_custom_sizes_strides(SizesStridesPolicy policy) { 
        

        
          
             python_custom_sizes_strides_ = static_cast<uint8_t>(policy); 
        

        
          
             refresh_sizes_strides_policy(); 
        

        
          
           } 
        
    
  


and then to refresh_sizes_strides_policy:

  
    
      pytorch/c10/core/TensorImpl.h
    
    
        Lines 2805 to 2813
      in
      56dd760
    
  
  
    

        
          
           void refresh_sizes_strides_policy() { 
        

        
          
             if (has_symbolic_sizes_strides_) { 
        

        
          
               sizes_strides_policy_ = 
        

        
          
                   static_cast<uint8_t>(SizesStridesPolicy::CustomSizes); 
        

        
          
             } else { 
        

        
          
               sizes_strides_policy_ = 
        

        
          
                   std::max(custom_sizes_strides_, python_custom_sizes_strides_); 
        

        
          
             } 
        

        
          
           } 
        
    
  


we see that this controls the sizes_strides_policy_, and also has handling based on has_symbolic_sizes_strides_. Note that sizes_strides_policy_ and has_symbolic_sizes_strides_ are separate
Meanwhile, Nested Tensor implements sizes via torch dispatch:
[TODO... more details, link to nt implementation]
Ideas



Repro:
import torch

values = torch.rand((8, 4))
offsets = torch.tensor([0, 2, 5, 6, 8])
nt = torch.nested.nested_tensor_from_jagged(values, offsets)
print(nt.shape)  # torch.Size([4, j2, 4])
print(nt._has_symbolic_sizes_strides)  # False

🐛 Describe the bug
How to repro:
comment out the lines below:

  
    
      pytorch/test/inductor/test_aot_inductor.py
    
    
        Lines 2322 to 2324
      in
      57a9a64

               is_skip=True 
        

        
          
           ), 
        
    
  


and run the following command:
$ python test/inductor/test_aot_inductor.py -k test_zero_grid_with_unbacked_symbols_abi_compatible_cpu_with_stack_allocation_and_minimal_arrayref_interface

While the test itself succeeds, the test runner segfaults before it exits.
Running it under gdb gives the following stack trace:
#0  0x00007fffb1caeb10 in ?? ()
#1  0x00007ffff68af896 in (anonymous namespace)::run (p=<optimized out>) at /opt/conda/conda-bld/gcc-compiler_1654084175708/work/gcc/libstdc++-v3/libsupc++/atexit_thread.cc:80
#2  (anonymous namespace)::run () at /opt/conda/conda-bld/gcc-compiler_1654084175708/work/gcc/libstdc++-v3/libsupc++/atexit_thread.cc:105

In particular, we are segfaulting when trying to run the destructor here: https://github.com/gcc-mirror/gcc/blob/releases/gcc-11/libstdc%2B%2B-v3/libsupc%2B%2B/atexit_thread.cc#L80
The destructor's address originally points to ~RAIIAtenTensorHandle() within model.so, but by the time we try to run it, model.so has already been unloaded; hence the segfault. Not sure why this is only being triggered by the minimal arrayref interface though.
Versions

gcc used to build PyTorch: 11.4.1

🐛 Describe the bug
The backward pass of ch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention is not deterministic for bfloat16 and float16 inputs. The function is deterministic for float32 backward passes, however. In particular the gradient wrt the query input is not deterministic (maybe the others aren't too but I did not find any inputs for which they weren't). Below is a minimal example.
import torch as ch

def set_seed(seed):
    ch.manual_seed(seed)
    ch.cuda.manual_seed(seed)
    ch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)
    ch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True
    ch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False
    ch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True
    ch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = True
    ch.backends.cudnn.enabled = True
    ch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)

def get_quantities(q, k, v, dtype):
    with ch.cuda.amp.autocast(dtype=dtype):
        y = ch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v,
                                                            attn_mask=None,
                                                            dropout_p=0,
                                                            is_causal=True) 
    ys = y.sum()
    ys.sum().backward()

    outputs = [y, q.grad, k.grad, v.grad]
    outputs = [v.clone().detach().cpu() for v in outputs]
    return list(zip(['y', 'grad q', 'grad k', 'grad v'], outputs))

def rand_tensor():
    v = ch.randn(32, 16, 511, 64, device='cuda')
    v.requires_grad_(True)
    return v

def main(dtype):
    for seed in range(3):
        set_seed(seed)
        q, k, v = rand_tensor(), rand_tensor(), rand_tensor()
        outputs1 = get_quantities(q, k, v, dtype)

        set_seed(seed)
        q, k, v = rand_tensor(), rand_tensor(), rand_tensor()
        
        outputs2 = get_quantities(q, k, v, dtype)
        failed = False
        for (n1, o1), (_, o2) in zip(outputs1, outputs2):
            max_diff = (o1-o2).absolute().max().item()
            if max_diff != 0:
                print(f'>> {dtype}: failed for seed', seed, 'with max diff',
                      max_diff, 'at tensor', n1)
                failed = True

    if not failed:
        print(f'>> {dtype}: all tests passed!')


main(ch.bfloat16)
main(ch.float32)
yields
>> torch.bfloat16: failed for seed 0 with max diff 0.0009765625 at tensor grad q
>> torch.bfloat16: failed for seed 1 with max diff 0.0009765625 at tensor grad q
>> torch.bfloat16: failed for seed 2 with max diff 0.00048828125 at tensor grad q
>> torch.float32: all tests passed!

>> torch.float16: failed for seed 1 with max diff 0.0001220703125 at tensor grad q
>> torch.float16: failed for seed 2 with max diff 0.000244140625 at tensor grad q

🐛 Describe the bug
If a module has overridden load_state_dict()/state_dict(), the corresponding compiled module may not work. I'm currently use a workaround like the following:
def my_load(self, state_dict, strict=True):
    self._orig_mod.load_state_dict(state_dict, strict)

model = torch.compile(model)
model.__class__.load_state_dict = my_load

    raise RuntimeError('Error(s) in loading state_dict for {}:\n\t{}'.format(
RuntimeError: Error(s) in loading state_dict for OptimizedModule:
	Missing key(s) in state_dict: "_orig_mod.linear.weight", "_orig_mod.linear.bias".

import torch


class M(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = torch.nn.Linear(3, 5)

    def state_dict(self):
        return {}

    def load_state_dict(self, state_dict):
        pass


module = M()
sd = module.state_dict()

compiled = torch.compile(module)
compiled.load_state_dict(sd)

nodes.bodyText:
This is really footgun-y and prevents us from easily adding new features. The main problems are:

torch.ops.namespace.foo is an OpOverloadPacket
the OpOverloadPacket caches all of the OpOverloads associated with it.
If someone defines a new OpOverload after accessing the OpOverloadPacket, it doesn't automatically get associated with the OpOverloadPacket

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Background
Many existing Large Language Models (LLMs) utilize FP16 during inference to improve performance. Downstream inference libraries, such as vllm, rely on fundamental operators in PyTorch, like F.Linear. Presently, PyTorch only supports two levels of FP16 GEMM, controlled by allow_fp16_reduced_precision_reduction. Both levels use FP32 as the computation accumulation data type.
Opportunity
Commodity NVIDIA RTX GPUs, such as the 3090 and 4090, show double throughput when doing FP16 GEMM with FP16 accumulation compared to FP32 accumulation. By benchmarking following simple perplexity test script, it can be demonstrated that using FP16 accumulation results in a 40% end-to-end speedup on 4090, with a minimal perplexity increase (0.0006) in LLM serving scenarios.
# from https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/perplexity
import torch
from tqdm import tqdm
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

name = "meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name,torch_dtype=torch.float16).cuda()
ds = load_dataset("wikitext", "wikitext-2-raw-v1", split="test")
encodings = tokenizer("\n\n".join(ds["text"]), return_tensors="pt")

max_length = 2048
stride = 1024
seq_len = encodings.input_ids.size(1)

nlls = []
prev_end_loc = 0
for begin_loc in tqdm(range(0, seq_len, stride)):
    end_loc = min(begin_loc + max_length, seq_len)
    trg_len = end_loc - prev_end_loc  # may be different from stride on last loop
    input_ids = encodings.input_ids[:, begin_loc:end_loc].to('cuda')
    target_ids = input_ids.clone()
    target_ids[:, :-trg_len] = -100

    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model(input_ids, labels=target_ids)
        neg_log_likelihood = outputs.loss

    nlls.append(neg_log_likelihood)
    prev_end_loc = end_loc
    if end_loc == seq_len:
        break

ppl = torch.exp(torch.stack(nlls).mean())
print(ppl)
Proposed Feature
Introduce a new API named torch.set_float16_matmul_precision to offer three levels of precision:


"highest": FP16 matmul uses FP32 as all the intermediate accumulation mode, which may lead to performance regression. This aligns with setting torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_fp16_reduced_precision_reduction to False.


"high" (default): FP16 matmul uses FP32 as the computation accumulation mode. This aligns with setting torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_fp16_reduced_precision_reduction to True, which is also the current default behavior.


"medium": FP16 matmul uses FP16 as the computation accumulation mode.


This feature enhancement aims to provide users with more control over the precision levels during FP16 matmul operations, catering to needs in inference scenarios
Alternatives
No response
Additional context
Migrated from #123157, make the feature more clear here.

nodes.bodyText:
📚 The doc issue
https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.PReLU.html#prelu
The doc shows that the prelu formula is: y = x >=0 ? x : ax  (1)
but according to the paper "Delving Deep into Rectifiers:Surpassing Human-Level Performance on ImageNet Classification",
the formula is: y = x >0 ? x : ax (2)
There are big difference when a is special number such as NaN or INF and x is 0, according to the formula (1), y = 0,
but according to the formula (2), y = NaN
Suggest a potential alternative/fix
Change the doc's formula to "y = x >0 ? x : a*x"

nodes.title: torch.compile dynamo fails indexing into array from internal mutable state

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
This is what numpy uses

ILP64 uses the 64-bit integer type (necessary for indexing large arrays, with more than 231-1 elements), whereas the LP64 libraries index arrays with the 32-bit integer type.

Also, is there any reason to not use libopenblas64-openmp-dev /libopenblas64-openmp?
Alternatives
None - current is 32-bit
Additional context
Xref JuliaLang/julia#4923

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
Description
In many APIs, there exists a parameter called eps, which is designed to be a small floating-point number. However, I have found that the code still runs when given a large integer value.
I believe this is a bug, as it contradicts the original purpose of eps.
Furthermore, when the value of eps is very large, it artificially inflates the denominator in some normalization algorithms, resulting in normalization outcomes that are very close to zero.
This might cause issues such as gradient vanishing, slower convergence, or poor model performance in practical applications.
Poc
Sample code to reproduce the problem:
input = torch.randn(5, 10)
m = torch.nn.InstanceNorm1d(num_features=5, eps=2018915490, affine=True)
output = m(input)
print(output)
The error message i got:

         -4.6150e-05, -8.2182e-06,  1.1602e-05, -1.1196e-05,  3.5870e-05],

Supplement
I initially observed this phenomenon with the torch.nn.InstanceNorm1d. And, upon verification, I found that similar occurrences are present in many other APIs.
Including:
torch.nn.InstanceNorm1d, torch.nn.InstanceNorm2d, torch.nn.InstanceNorm3d,
torch.nn.LazyInstanceNorm1d, torch.nn.LazyInstanceNorm2d, torch.nn.LazyInstanceNorm3d,
torch.nn.GroupNorm, torch.nn.PairwiseDistance,
torch.nn.BatchNorm1d, torch.nn.BatchNorm2d, torch.nn.BatchNorm3d,
torch.nn.LazyBatchNorm1d, torch.nn.LazyBatchNorm2d, torch.nn.LazyBatchNorm3d,
torch.nn.LayerNorm, torch.nn.functional.normalize, torch.nn.functional.gaussian_nll_loss
torch.nn.GaussianNLLLoss, torch.nn.utils.spectral_norm

Sample code to repoduce the problem with torch.nn.utils.spectral_norm:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.utils as nn_utils

input = torch.randn(3, 10)
linear = nn.Linear(in_features=10, out_features=5)
linear = nn_utils.spectral_norm(linear, eps=2018915490)
output = linear(input)
print(output)
The error message i got:
tensor([[nan, nan, nan, nan, nan],
        [nan, nan, nan, nan, nan],
        [nan, nan, nan, nan, nan]], grad_fn=<AddmmBackward0>)

Expectation
I suggest implementing a range check for the eps parameter to avoid the inadvertent passing of large integers without a warning, leading to suboptimal results.

🐛 Describe the bug
We fail to do fake tensor propagation when using TorchAO quant with freezing pass. Actually, the number of frozen parameters is not as expected. For example, we have two linears L1 and L2. The frozen  parameters are supposed to be weight of L1, scale of L1, weight of L2 and scale of L2. But in fact, we only get two frozen parameters --- two qtensors. The tensor subclass Int8DynamicallyQuantizedLinearWeight in TorchAO is a qtensor, possessing int_data and q_scales as attributes. It seems to be some bugs in parameter flattening, mistaking qtensor of L1 as weight of L1, and qtensor of L2 as scale of L1.
Reproduced code with flag TORCHINDUCTOR_FREEZING=1:
import torch
from torchao.quantization import quant_api
 
class M(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(
        self,
        use_bias,
        post_op_algo,
    ):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear1 = torch.nn.Linear(16, 16, use_bias)
        self.linear2 = torch.nn.Linear(16, 16, use_bias)
 
    def forward(self, x):
        temp = self.linear1(x)
        temp = self.linear2(temp)
 
        return temp

        _ = compiler_mode(*inputs)
        output = compiler_mode(*inputs)

    def forward(self, x, y):
        return self.linear1(x) + self.linear1(y)

from torch.utils import ThroughputBenchmark
model = torch.compile(SimpleM().bfloat16())
x1 = torch.randn(100, 100).bfloat16()

🐛 Describe the bug
If a state dict contains a valid key (e.g. "fc1.weight") and an unexpected key that starts with the valid key (e.g. "fc1.weight.bad_key"), then load_state_dict() does not handle this in the way that I'd expect.
Code to reproduce:
import torch

class SimpleModel(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = torch.nn.Linear(5, 10)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc1(x)


def try_load_state_dict(model: SimpleModel, state_dict: dict[str, torch.Tensor], strict: bool):
    print(f"state_dict.keys(): {state_dict.keys()}")
    print(f"strict={strict}")

    print(f"Calling load_state_dict()...")
    try:
        load_result = model.load_state_dict(state_dict, strict=strict)
        print(f"load_result.missing_keys: {load_result.missing_keys}")
        print(f"load_result.unexpected_keys: {load_result.unexpected_keys}")

Ideally, we need these guards. A smaller example is
import torch

def gn(x, use_1=None):
    if use_1:
        return x + 1
    return x + 2

@torch.compile(backend="eager")
def fn(x):
    return gn(x)


fn(torch.randn(4))

# Should we guard on defaults for inlined function?
gn.__defaults__= ("blah",)

fn(torch.randn(4))

This is unlikely to happen, i.e., users do not change the fn defaults. But Dynamo is trying to be conservative here and putting guards.
Let me know if one feels strongly about deleting these guards.

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Today we don't compile the optimizer if a closure is present and fall back to eager. The main reason for this is that a graph break in the top level optimizer step call will not allow dynamo to properly initialize the optimizer (since it will no longer interpret that frame). I'm publishing this issue to track if this feature is desirable for users.
Ex.
import torch     
weight = Parameter(torch.randn((10, 5, 2), device=device, dtype=dtype)[..., 0])
bias = Parameter(torch.randn((10, 2), device=device, dtype=dtype)[..., 0])
input = torch.randn(5, device=device, dtype=dtype)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([weight, bias], **optim_input.kwargs)
schedulers = [s(optimizer) for s in (schedulers_constructor if schedulers_constructor else [])]

def closure():
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = (weight.mv(input) + bias).pow(2).sum()
    loss.backward()
    return loss

optim.step(closure)
The current workaround is to call the closure outside of the optimizer like so:
Ex.
import torch     
weight = Parameter(torch.randn((10, 5, 2), device=device, dtype=dtype)[..., 0])
bias = Parameter(torch.randn((10, 2), device=device, dtype=dtype)[..., 0])
input = torch.randn(5, device=device, dtype=dtype)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([weight, bias], **optim_input.kwargs)
schedulers = [s(optimizer) for s in (schedulers_constructor if schedulers_constructor else [])]

def closure():
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = (weight.mv(input) + bias).pow(2).sum()
    loss.backward()
    return loss

closure()
optim.step()
If compiling with closure would be helpful to you please comment below with your use case.

🚀 [RFC] Cuda support matrix for Release 2.4
Opening this RFC to discuss CUDA version support for future PyTorch releases:
Option 1 - CUDA 11 and CUDA 12:
CUDA 11.8, CUDNN 8.9.7.29
CUDA 12.4, CUDNN 8.9.7.29 - Version hosted on pypi
Option 2 - CUDA 12:
CUDA 12.1, CUDNN 8.9.7.29
CUDA 12.4, CUDNN 8.9.7.29 - Version hosted on pypi
Option 3
CUDA 11.8, CUDNN 8.9.7.29
CUDA 12.1, CUDNN 8.9.7.29 - Version hosted on pypi, as stable
CUDA 12.4, CUDNN 8.9.7.29 - Experimental version
(Please note CUDNN version listed here 8.9.7.29 is not final, we may upgrade it for 2.4 release)
One advantage of Option 1 is the fact that older cuda driver is not compatible with CUDA 12 hence people with older drivers will benefit latest pytorch.
Please refer to:
https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/cuda-compatibility/index.html#minor-version-compatibility

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Update: all tasks below have in progress PRs currently!
In test_cuda.py and test_torch.py, we have the following optimizer tests that should be migrated to use the new OptimizerInfo infrastructure. (See any of the tests in TestOptimRenewed for how to apply OptimizerInfos.) The basic structure to expect for an updated test will look like:
    @optims([optim for optim in optim_db if ...], dtypes=[torch.float32])
    def test_name(self, device, dtype, optim_info):
        optim_cls = optim_info.optim_cls
        optim_inputs = optim_info.optim_inputs_func(device=device)
        for optim_input in optim_inputs:
            params = ...
            // processing, like updating grads

            optimizer = optim_cls(params, ..., **optim_input.kwargs)

            // the actual test
            ...
            self.assertEquals(...)

test_cuda.py:

 test_grad_scaling_autocast_fused_optimizers will be addressed in #124904 and by @SandishKumarHN
 test_graph_grad_scaling
 test_graph_optims
 test_graph_optims_with_explicitly_capturable_param_groups
 test_graph_scaling_fused_optimizers

test_torch.py: #125538

 tests that call _grad_scaling_autocast_test can be combined into one test
 test_params_invalidated_with_grads_invalidated_between_unscale_and_step should be tested on more configurations (like SGD fused!)
there are many other tests that test just one optimizer config that we can leave for now.

Feel free to take up one or a subset of those tests to migrate--edit your username next to the checklist to claim an item to submit PRs for!
